_comment: The 'AI Innovator (Cost-Bounded)' custom role.
READ THIS FIRST - WHAT THIS ROLE CAN AND CANNOT DO
Azure RBAC is a list of resource-provider OPERATIONS. It cannot inspect
the SKU, size, capacity, replica count or throughput in a request body.
There is therefore NO role definition - built-in or custom - that can
express 'may create a Fabric capacity, but not an F2048'.
Microsoft states the division of labour directly:
'Azure Policy evaluates state by examining properties on resources that
are represented in Resource Manager... Azure RBAC focuses on managing
user actions at different scopes.'
- https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/governance/policy/overview
So the guardrail is a PAIR:
THIS ROLE          decides WHICH resource types may be created
THE POLICY PACK    decides HOW EXPENSIVE each one may be
Deploying this role without the SKU-ceiling policies in ../policies/ hands
someone the ability to create an F2048 Fabric capacity and a 12x12 AI
Search service. Do not ship half of this.
DESIGN: ALLOW-LIST, NOT DENY-LIST
Actions are an explicit allow-list plus '*/read'. Anything not named is
denied by omission. That is deliberate. A deny-list ('*' minus the
expensive things) silently admits every service Azure ships next quarter,
which is the opposite of what was asked for. The trade-off is that adding
a genuinely-needed service requires editing ROLE_ALLOWED_PROVIDERS or
ROLE_EXTRA_PROVIDERS - a deliberate, reviewable act.
This file is a TEMPLATE. Invoke-AiGuardrails.ps1 expands the __TOKEN__
placeholders from .env and writes the real definition. Do not assign this
file directly.
NOT-ACTIONS: the four rules below are the ones that matter even inside the
allow-list, because each is a way to escape the guardrail rather than use
a resource:
1. Authorization write/delete + elevateAccess - otherwise the holder
grants themselves Owner and the whole design is decorative.
2. Consumption + CostManagement write - otherwise they can delete the
budget and the anomaly alert that watch them.
3. CognitiveServices commitmentPlans write - a commitment plan is a
committed spend decision, not an innovation one.
4. Subscription cancel/enable and deploymentStacks deny-setting -
inherited from the built-in Contributor NotActions for the same
reasons Microsoft excludes them there.
A KNOWN, DELIBERATE TRADE-OFF: Microsoft.Insights/* is granted, because a
team building an AI workload genuinely needs Application Insights. That
same grant would let them delete the action group and alert rule that
watch their spend - usually not maliciously, usually somebody tidying up a
resource they do not recognise. Rather than cripple legitimate alerting
work with a notActions entry, the playbook puts a CanNotDelete lock on
those two specific resources. The role cannot remove it, because
Microsoft.Authorization/*/write is already denied above.
